name: Rukai
confidence_why: Li 1973, the one first-hand grammar of the Tanan dialect, states that every content word is stressed on its last syllable (bavá, tuLú, taLagí) apart from interrogatives and the monosyllabic articles, Li 1977 repeats that Tanan stress is mostly final once the echo vowels are left out of the transcription, and Blust 2013's Tanan forms (abó, comáy, cakí, ɭikoláw) fit that rule, but Li 1977 and Blust 2013 also call Rukai stress phonemic and the other dialects place it differently (Mantauran on the first syllable of the stem, Budai and Labuan mostly on the penult), so the record rests on a single fieldworker's description. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Li 1973.

catalog_quote: [Li 1973: 21] Every content word in Rukai is stressed on the last syllable, e.g. [bavá] 'wine', [tuLú] 'three', [taLagí] 'friend'. This can be accounted for by a phonological rule that assigns stress to the final syllable of a word (see 3.9). There are two general types of exceptions to the stress rule. All interrogative words receive a stress on the penultimate syllable, e.g. [ʔíya] 'how much' (vs. [ʔiyá] 'do', [mikakúwa] 'how', [manɨ́ma] 'what', [anɨ́a] 'who', [lwíga] 'when (future)', [kwíga] 'when (past)', [ínu] 'where'. These have to be treated as lexical exceptions. ... The monosyllabic articles [ka], [sa], [ku] and [ki] (cf. 4.2.2.2) are also exceptions in that they do not bear stress. One further exception: [kuíya] 'there (far)'. [Li 1973: 63, sec. 3.9] (2) FINAL STRESS ASSIGNMENT [+voc, -cons] --> [+stress] / __ ({[+cons] / [-voc, -cons]}) # ... (5) ECHO VOWEL ADDITION Ø --> [+voc, +high, αback, βround, -stress] / [+voc, αback, βround] [+cons] __ {# / [+cons] / [+voc, +high]} ... (8) EMPHATIC or QUESTION STRESS [-stress] --> [+stress] / __ # [Li 1973: 52] (4)(a) It makes stress more predictable: stress mostly falls on the final syllable;

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Tanan (Taromak) dialect described by Li, stress falls on the final syllable of every content word, assigned by rule; the final syllable is counted without the optional 'echo vowel' that can follow a word-final consonant (Li leaves echo vowels out of underlying forms precisely so that stress is predictable and final; if they are counted, consonant-final words surface as penult-stressed). Interrogative words are lexically marked for penultimate stress; the monosyllabic articles are unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Interrogatives (ʔíya 'how much', mikakúwa 'how', manɨ́ma 'what', anɨ́a 'who', lwíga/kwíga 'when', ínu 'where') take penultimate stress as lexical exceptions; articles ka, sa, ku, ki bear no stress; kuíya 'there (far)'; apparent pairs like [taí] 'taro' vs [tái] 'family' are resolved as tai vs tay (final /y, w/) rather than as stress exceptions (p. 22). Li 1977: 8, 26 (same author) later calls stress phonemic in all dialects except Mantauran and only 'mostly' final in Tanan; Blust 2013: 173, 666-667 lists cross-dialect stress disagreements (Tanan/Tona abó vs Budai ábo 'ash').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (content words in citation/isolation); Li's rule applies to the phonological word as represented without echo vowels. Dialect-specific: Tanan. Other dialects per Li 1977 (pp. 8, 26, 85-86): Budai, Tona, Maga, Labuan mostly penultimate with contrastive (phonemic) stress; Mantauran non-phonemic, on the first syllable of the stem.
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1973 describes the Tanan (Taromak/Tarumak) dialect of Taitung, Glottolog dialect tana1287 (main informant Te-tz'u Lin, p. 10). Stress placement is dialect-dependent in Rukai: Li 1977 (pp. 8, 26, 85-86) states stress is phonemic in all dialects except Mantauran (mant1271, stem-initial), mostly final in Tanan (if echo vowels are omitted) but mostly penultimate in Budai (buda1252), Tona (tona1238), Maga (maga1265) and Labuan (labu1252); Blust 2013: 173, 666-667 confirms contrastive, cross-dialectally disagreeing stress. A language-level reading for ruka1240 should therefore be flagged as dialect-specific (Tanan = fixed: final syllable by rule; Budai etc. = mostly penult, lexically contrastive).

new_statements.quote: p. 255: "Main stress in Budai Rukai falls on either the heavy penult or the antepenult of a word, depending on the weight of the penult. It is apparent that Budai stress is [+Quantity Sensitive] in the typology of stress. In other words, syllable weight plays a crucial role in the assignment of stress. Word stress never falls on the final syllable in Budai Rukai, except a restricted number of heavy monosyllabic roots." p. 251 (45a): "in monosyllabic roots, stress falls on the nucleus of the syllable; in disyllabic roots, main stress falls on the penult; in trisyllabic or longer roots, if the penultimate syllable is light, main stress falls on the antepenult; if the penult is heavy, main stress falls on the penult."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records Rukai as fixed final stress (Li 1973, which describes the Tanan dialect). Chen 2006 describes the Budai dialect of the same Glottolog language and finds a different placement and type: quantity-sensitive penult/antepenult with final-syllable extrametricality, never final in polysyllables. Chen does not dispute Li's final stress for Tanan (she restates it, p. 258) — the disagreement is a dialect split inside ruka1240, not a competing analysis of the same variety. A language-level 'fixed final' record therefore over-generalises Tanan to all of Rukai.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Budai Rukai (author's own fieldwork): final syllable extrametrical (NONFINALITY), moraic trochees built right-to-left, End Rule Right. Result: disyllables stress the penult; words of three or more syllables stress the penult if it is heavy (long vowel or diphthong; no codas exist) and otherwise the antepenult; stress is never final except on heavy monosyllabic roots. Vowel-length contrast surfaces only in the penult (long vowels elsewhere shorten). Prefixes, infixes, ligatures/construction markers are outside the stress domain; suffixed forms take antepenultimate stress; in prefixed disyllabic roots stress stays on the root penult. Stress is predictable at word level and does not distinguish word classes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: pp. 253-254: 'Secondary stress falls on remaining heavy syllables, and on every other light syllable counting from right to the left' (attested in words of four/five or more syllables, e.g. lupàkaváal 'the day after tomorrow', tàraámar 'one month'); in complex numerals the rightmost content word takes primary stress, earlier content words secondary.
new_statements.exceptions: Heavy monosyllabic roots carry (final) stress; construction markers ka/sa/ku/ki, ligatures, prefixes and infixes never stressed (extrametrical); imperatives carry a word-level pitch accent rather than final stress; sec. 6.1.1: speakers in contact with Northern Paiwan (Southern Sanhe village, some middle-aged Budai villagers) shift antepenultimate stress to the penult regardless of weight (válisi ~ valísi 'tooth', takurápa ~ takurapá 'toad') = 'release from extrametricality', a contact pattern; older mountain-village speakers keep the canonical pattern. The author also reports (pp. 249-250, 258, 261) Li 1973/1977a: Tanan Rukai stress falls on the last syllable (final once echo vowels are counted) and shifts onto following personal markers; Li 1977a: stress phonemic in all dialects except Mantauran (stem-initial); Li 1995 wordlist: Budai stress mostly penultimate, less often final or antepenult; Zeitoun 2000: Budai penultimate, a few antepenultimate, no final; Ross 1992: Budai CVCVC accent unpredictable (rejected by Chen).
new_statements.identity_note: Chen 2006 describes Budai Rukai (Budai, Haocha and Southern Sanhe villages, Pingtung), which Li 1995 (as cited) calls the most representative Rukai dialect; the catalog's existing statement is from Li 1973 on Tanan Rukai. Both are dialects under Glottolog ruka1240. Chen's sec. 6.1.1 data on penultimate 'contact stress' come from Budai speakers in frequent contact with Northern Paiwan and are explicitly not the canonical pattern.

tone_statements.quote: Tonal alignment in Budai Rukai happens at a level described by Macaulay (2021, 2023 as the IP (intonational phrase). This phrase, in all utterance types studied, ends with a final low boundary tone L% … Each IP in Budai Rukai surfaces with one pitch accent, regardless of the number of accented syllables within the IP. … It is to the final prominent syllable in the IP that the pitch accent attaches. … The pitch accent melody in declarative utterances (and words in isolation) in Budai Rukai is (L+)H*, in which the nuclear H* surfaces on the prominent syllable.

readall_conflicts: For context only (not from a work in this task's list): the earlier reading's notes in record Li 1977 (BIHP 48(1), p. 8) as stating that stress is phonemic in all Rukai dialects except Mantauran, where it falls on the first syllable of the stem, whereas the catalog's Li 1973 statement (Tanan/Budai-based description) gives final-syllable stress on every content word with listed exceptions. That dialect-level divergence (Mantauran initial vs. other dialects final, and 'phonemic' vs. rule-predictable) is already on record from the earlier reading and is not resolved or changed here. Blust 1997 'Rukai stress revisited' (Oceanic Linguistics 36(2)) remains unobtained (paywalled) per the same notes. The catalog's 'Rukai = fixed final stress' rests on Li 1973 (Tanan dialect). Chen 2006, from first-hand fieldwork and acoustic measurement, shows Budai Rukai is quantity-sensitive: heavy penult stressed, otherwise antepenult, final syllable extrametrical, never final stress in polysyllables (pp. 251, 255, 315-318). Chen herself accepts Li's Tanan final stress and cites Li 1977a that Mantauran has stem-initial stress and that stress is 'phonemic' in the other dialects; she also notes Li 1995 (Budai mostly penultimate) and Zeitoun 2000 (Budai penultimate, some antepenultimate, no final), and rejects Ross 1992's 'unpredictable' Budai accent. tone.quote: Stress has been difficult to analyze and it would certainly deserve an in-depth study that I am unable to provide here. Stress usually falls on the first syllable as in tamatama [támatama] 'middle-aged man', aan [áan] 'house', koap [kóap] 'sock' and shifts to the first syllable if the base is prefixed, e.g. titina [títina] 'middle-aged woman' > aitina [áitina] 'middle-aged women'. There is also a secondary stress in multisyllabic words [...]. Stress has been treated as non-phonemic in earlier works (cf. Tsuchida 1976 and Li 1977b), and I tentatively follow this treatment here. [...] Intonation is another phonological area that needs further investigation, as I did not collect any data related to this topic.
